name: Marco Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I look after a till system that independent pubs and restaurants use, at a software company of about fifty people in an old converted mill. It's a desktop program, written in C#, and my job is keeping it running when a landlord rings on a Friday night because the card machine won't talk to it. I like that the customers are real small businesses, people I could go and have a pint with. What wears me out is management always chasing the next shiny thing instead of fixing what we've got.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Anna, who's a teaching assistant at the primary school, and we rent a small terraced house near my parents. Sundays are church and then lunch at Mum and Dad's, every week. We've got less than a month saved, because we're paying for the wedding ourselves, and my pay's on the low side for the job, but there's not much else round here unless I commute two hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I've thought all along, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that a lot of money got wasted chasing a fashion. At work I'd say let's get back to fixing the till system for the people who pay us. I'm not one for posting, but I'd say it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, but our money's still tight with the wedding coming. The firm lost three pub chains last year when pubs closed, so the business isn't exactly booming. If they cut anyone, I'm not the star of the team, so it could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and keep away from the AI coding tool the manager keeps mentioning. I'd do the Friday night on-call for extra money, and we'd keep the wedding at the church hall rather than a hotel. I'd also ask Dad if he needs a hand on his electrical jobs some Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm relieved about AI and worried about money, and the money worry was here first. Those are two different things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine parts of your job might AI take even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the support emails, the ones that are always the same three answers. That's an hour a day. I'd actually be fine with a machine sending the 'have you restarted it' reply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think should happen with the pubs that keep closing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lower taxes on them, honestly, and less paperwork. They're the centre of a village. If they close, my customers close, and so does my job.

say: I'd say a lot of **money got wasted** chasing a fashion.
I'd say we should get back to fixing the **till system** for paying customers.
think: Money's still **tight** with the wedding coming, whatever happens with AI.
The firm **lost three pub chains** last year, and I'm not the star of the team.
do: Carry on and avoid the **AI coding tool** the manager keeps mentioning.
Take the **Friday night on-call** for extra money.
Ask Dad for **Saturday work** on his electrical jobs.
feel: **Relieved** about AI but **worried** about money, which was there first.
S0.quote: I'm relieved about AI and worried about money, and the money worry was here first.
fieldNote: His worry ties to **pub closures**, which shrink his firm's customer base.
He blames **taxes and paperwork** on pubs, fitting his free-market views.
His dad's **electrical work** is a quiet fallback already in the picture.

steps.text: Keep maintaining the C# till system without AI tools
Do Saturday electrical work with Dad for extra cash
Hold the wedding at the church hall instead of a hotel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. Coding's on that list, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses should be free to use it, but they owe their staff the chance to learn. I wouldn't want the government stepping in and making a mess. At church I'd probably say it's a time for families to pull together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the team gets smaller, and I'm the one who's never touched the AI. My only advantage is that pub landlords are slow to change, so the old till system might hang on a few years. But the people who write the new one won't be people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself sit the AI training, even though I'd hate it. I'd start doing Saturday jobs with Dad properly, learning the trade, so I've got something real. Anna and I would keep the wedding small and keep a bit back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit ashamed that I've been so stubborn about the tools. Mostly worried about the wedding year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steve, who's been on support for twenty years and knows every pub owner by name. He's even worse with computers than me, which is saying something for a software firm. He's got three kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for any help from outside, if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then church. Not the government, if I can help it. My dad says he'd rather pay me to pull cable than see me on benefits, and I feel the same.

say: I'd say firms should be **free to use AI** but owe staff a chance to learn.
I'd say it's a time for **families to pull together**, not for government meddling.
think: The team shrinks, and I'm the one who's **never touched** the AI.
**Slow pub landlords** may keep the old till system going a few years.
do: Sit the **AI training** even though I'd hate it.
Learn the **electrical trade** properly on Saturdays with Dad.
Keep the wedding **small** and hold some money back.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit **ashamed** of being so stubborn.
S1.quote: My dad says he'd rather pay me to pull cable than see me on benefits, and I feel the same.
fieldNote: He blames his **own stubbornness** more than the technology.
**Family and church** come before any state help.
His bet is that **slow customers** buy him a few years.

steps.text: Sit the firm's AI coding training course
Work Saturdays with Dad learning electrical installation
Keep the church hall wedding small and save the rest

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before we'd have a kid, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a test for families and communities, and that we'll get through it the way people always have. I'd still be wary of the government taking over everything. At church I'd help organise something for people losing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm out. My job is code and phone calls, and the AI would do both better and cheaper by 2028. The one bit of luck is that wiring houses is hands-on, and the robots for that are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a proper electrical apprenticeship with Dad straight away, even though the pay is worse, while I still have the till job in the evenings. We'd move the wedding forward and keep it tiny, maybe just family at church. We'd stop all spending except rent, food and the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but not lost. I've got Dad's trade to fall back on, and that's more than most people at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years of electrical work, then robots. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe people still want a human in their house. I'd pray about it, which I know sounds old-fashioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Anna's parents about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll provide for her, whatever it takes. Her dad's a builder, so he'd understand. He'd probably offer me work too.

say: I'd call it a **test for families** and communities, and say we'll get through.
I'd stay **wary of government** taking over everything.
think: My job is **code and phone calls**, so the AI replaces me by 2028.
Wiring houses is **hands-on**, and robots for that are three years behind.
do: Start an **electrical apprenticeship** with Dad straight away, coding in the evenings.
Move the wedding **forward** and keep it tiny.
Cut spending to **rent, food** and the car.
feel: **Frightened** but **not lost**, thanks to Dad's trade.
S2.quote: My job is code and phone calls, and the AI would do both better and cheaper by 2028.
fieldNote: He has a **real fallback** in his dad's trade, which keeps this from panic.
Faith and **providing for Anna** shape how he talks about the future.
He has **no plan past 2031**, and says he'd pray about it.

steps.text: Start a full electrical apprenticeship with Dad's firm
Bring the wedding forward to a small family church service
Cut spending to rent, food and the car
Take building work from Anna's father if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare and people should take responsibility for themselves. I'd want more apprenticeships, not more benefits. I'd say it at church and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep the till job for three years or so, and then it's over. That's enough time to get qualified as an electrician if I start now. By 2034, when the robots come, I'd be thirty-five and hopefully have a few years in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the part-time electrical qualification at the college and do Saturdays with Dad. We'd have the wedding as planned next summer, small. We'd try for a baby a bit later than we wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can see a path. Five years is enough to do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why later for a baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to know I'm earning before a child comes. My parents had nothing when I was born, and Mum still talks about it. I don't want that for Anna.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the AI tools at work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if they made me. But I'd rather put my effort into something that lasts. Learning an AI tool that replaces me in five years seems backwards.

say: I'd say there's time, and people should **take responsibility** for themselves and prepare.
I'd call for **more apprenticeships**, not more benefits, at church and at the pub.
think: The till job lasts **three years** or so, then it's over.
That's enough time to get **qualified** as an electrician if I start now.
do: Sign up for a **part-time electrical** qualification at the college.
Hold a small wedding next summer and **wait a bit** for a baby.
S3.quote: Learning an AI tool that replaces me in five years seems backwards.
fieldNote: He uses the five years for a **clear trade switch** to electrician.
He'd **delay a baby** until his income feels safe, tied to his parents' story.
He'd only learn the **AI tools** if forced, seeing them as a dead end for him.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time electrical qualification at the college
Wait a couple of years before trying for a baby
Keep the till support job for about three years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so nobody can claim they weren't warned. People should plan, save and learn a trade if they need to. I'd want the government to stay out of the way and let firms train people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably keep doing what I'm doing for a good few years. The till system might even outlast that, because pubs are slow. I'd start the electrical course around year three or four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding and try for kids in the next couple of years. I'd keep the till job and keep Saturdays with Dad going. I'd save properly, aiming for three months in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a small worry. Ten years is long enough that I'd probably not think about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'm not good with change. But Dad would push me, and Anna would too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own kids, if they were growing up in this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my kids to learn something with their hands and something with their heads. And to go to church, honestly. That doesn't go out of date.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, so nobody can say they weren't warned.
I'd want government to stay **out of the way** and let firms train people.
think: I'd keep doing my job for a **good few years**, since pubs are slow.
I'd start the **electrical course** around year three or four.
do: Have the wedding and try for **kids** in the next couple of years.
Keep the **till job** and Saturdays with Dad.
S4.quote: I'd want my kids to learn something with their hands and something with their heads.
fieldNote: With ten years his **own job** feels safe, so the worry stays in the background.
His **family plans** go ahead as normal.
He admits **Dad and Anna** would have to push him to move.

steps.text: Marry Anna and try for children within two years
Keep the till support job and Saturday electrical work
Save three months of bills in the bank

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit in our wedding year. What would help is more apprenticeships, paid properly, and lower taxes on small businesses like the pubs, so there's still work around here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. When things change this fast, a lot of people round here will turn to church, not to a website. That matters more than people think.

headlineQuote: When things change this fast, a lot of people round here will turn to church, not to a website.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old** developer supporting a till system for independent pubs and restaurants.
He's engaged to Anna, a **teaching assistant**, and pays for the wedding himself.
He never uses AI, prefers **family and church** to state help, and favours apprenticeships.
His fallback is his dad's **electrical trade**, which gives him a path in every scenario.
His mood goes from uneasy to **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would hit in their wedding year.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower taxes** on small businesses like pubs.
